en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question of Inference.
5. The Question on Dreams “Venerable Nāgasena, in this world men and women see dreams—both auspicious and evil;
some they have seen before and others not; some they have done before and others not; some are peaceful and others fearful.”
“Whether far or near, whether of many kinds or thousands of colors, they are seen; what indeed is this so-called dream, and who is it that sees it?
“This is a sign, Great King, called a dream, which comes within the range of the mind.”
There are these four, O Great King, who see dreams: one with a wind disorder sees a dream; one with a bile disorder sees a dream;
one with a phlegm disorder sees a dream; and one sees a dream through the influence of deities.
One sees a dream from habitual practice, and one sees a dream as a foretoken. Therein, O Great King, that which is a dream as a foretoken—
“He sees it; that alone is the truth, and everything else is false.

“Venerable Nāgasena, when one sees a dream from a previous omen, does his own mind go there and investigate that sign, or does that sign come into the range of the mind, or does someone else come and report it to him?”
“Great King, it is not that his mind goes of its own accord to investigate that sign, nor does anyone else come and report it to him; rather, that very sign comes into the range of the mind.

Great King, it is just as a mirror does not go anywhere of its own accord to seek out a reflection, nor does anyone else bring a reflection and place it upon the mirror; rather, a reflection comes from somewhere or other and enters the range of the mirror.”

“In the same way, great king, it is not that the mind goes of its own accord to investigate that sign, nor does anyone else come and report it; rather, from wherever the sign comes, it enters the range of the mind.
“Venerable Nāgasena, as for that mind which sees a dream, does that mind know: ‘Such indeed will be the result—either security or fear’?”
“Indeed, Great King, that mind does not know: ‘Such will be the result—either security or danger. But when a sign has arisen, it tells others; then they explain the meaning from that.
“Pray, Venerable Nāgasena, show me the reason for this.
“Just as, Great King, moles, pustules, or skin eruptions arise on the body for the sake of gain or loss,”
“Whether it be for fame or infamy, for blame or praise, or for pleasure or pain—do those boils, Great King, arise with the conscious intention: ‘We shall accomplish such-and-such a purpose’?
“No indeed, venerable sir. Whatever kind of place those boils arise in, the fortune-tellers, seeing those boils there, declare: ‘Such-and-such will be the result.’”
“In the same way, great king, that mind which sees a dream does not know,
‘Such will be the result— either security or fear. But when the omen has arisen, it tells it to others,
and then they explain its meaning.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, does he who sees a dream see it while sleeping or while waking?
“Great King, he who sees a dream does not see it while sleeping, nor does he see it while waking.
Rather, when torpor has descended but the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has not yet reached [its usual state], in that interval one sees a dream.”
"Great King, when one is overcome by drowsiness, the mind has entered the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). When the mind has entered the life-continuum, it does not function.
When the mind does not function, it does not discern pleasure or pain. For one who does not discern, there is no dream;
one sees a dream only when the mind is functioning."
Just as, great king, in the darkness of a dim light, no reflection is seen even in a perfectly clean mirror;

even so, great king, when the mind is overcome by sloth and has entered the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), although the body remains standing, the mind is inactive. When the mind is inactive, one does not see a dream.
Just as the mirror, great king, so should the body be regarded.
As darkness is, so should drowsiness be regarded;
as light is, so should the mind be regarded.

Or again, Great King, just as when the sun is covered by mist its radiance is not seen, and though the solar rays are indeed present, they do not function; and because the solar rays do not function, there is no light.

In the same way, Great King, the mind of one overcome by drowsiness has entered the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); when the mind has entered the life-continuum, it does not function, and when the mind does not function, one does not see a dream.
Great King, the body should be regarded as like the sun, and drowsiness should be regarded as like a veil of mist.
Just as the sun’s ray, so should the mind be regarded.

Great King, even though the body exists, the mind does not function in two cases: in one who is overcome by torpor and has entered the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and in one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (nirodhasamāpatti); even though the body exists, the mind does not function.
When one is awake, O Great King, the mind becomes restless, exposed, manifest, and unsteady;
for such a mind, the sign does not enter.
Just as, O Great King, those who desire secrecy avoid a man who is exposed, manifest, and unrestrained;
“In the same way, Great King, for one who is awake, the divine purpose does not come within range; therefore, one who is awake does not see a dream.

Or again, Great King, just as for a monk of broken livelihood, of improper conduct, with evil friends, of immoral character, lazy, and of weak energy, the wholesome states conducive to enlightenment do not come within range;
even so, Great King, for one who is awake, the divine purpose does not come within range, and therefore one who is awake does not see a dream.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, does drowsiness have a beginning, a middle, and an end?
“Yes, Great King, drowsiness has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
“What is the beginning, what is the middle, and what is the end?”
“Great king, that which is the constriction, the envelopment, the weakness, the dullness, and the unworkability of the body—this is the beginning of drowsiness.
Great king, when one overcome by restless sleep remains in a state of intermittent wakefulness—this is the middle of drowsiness.
The movement into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is its end.”
"Having entered the middle [state], O Great King, and overcome by drowsiness, one sees a dream.

Just as someone, O Great King, who is of restrained conduct, concentrated in mind, established in the Dhamma, and of unshakable intelligence—having abandoned curiosity and noise—enters the depths of a forest and contemplates a subtle matter, yet does not fall into sloth there; he..."
Therein, one who is concentrated and one-pointed in mind penetrates a subtle meaning.
In the same way, Great King, it is not one who is awake and has fallen into sleep, nor one who is in the middle [of the night] overcome by the drowsiness of a monkey, who sees a dream.
Just as, Great King, the sound of a festival is to be regarded, so should waking be regarded.
"Just as the secluded forest is to be seen, so too is one overcome by monkey-sleep;

just as he, having abandoned the clamor of curiosity and avoided sloth, being in a state of equanimity, penetrates a subtle meaning, even so does one who is awake and not fallen into sloth see a dream while overcome by monkey-sleep.
"Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it."
The Fifth Question on Dreams.
